title: Simplifying RAG Document Pipelines with Multimodal Embeddings [PyCon DE & PyData 2026]

segments.text: Thank you everyone for joining. So the
topic of my talk today will be
simplifying rack pipelines with
multimodel embeddings. So first I'm
machine learning engineer at cyaners.
We're a small consulting company and in
that role I do all sorts of projects in
the genai or data science lately a lot
building rack system or agentic systems
in general.
So first, while I'm sure most of you
already know what RAG or retrieval
augmented generation is, just to get
everyone on the same page, retrieval
augmented generation is a concept where
you enhance language models, large
language models by integrating external
knowledge to reduce hallucination and
incorporate up-to-date information
without the need of retraining. So you
basically see it here. You start with
your input query to your to the language
model. And before passing it to the
language model, you query your vector
database which stores all your um
external information and you retrieve
the most relevant documents and then you
p basically pass the input query and
augment it by these relevant documents
and pass both of them to the language
model which then generates the output.
So the idea is basically to take away so
to not rely on the language model to
actually have the information but to
give it all the information and then to
mainly use it as summarization tool in
the end.
The main [snorts] question now is how do
you get your data into the vector
database
for this you use the so-called ingestion
pipeline which is the integral part of
any rag system. So this is the
processing layer that turns raw
documents into embeddings which are then
which then can be stored in your vector
database.
The core part now is that most embedding
models especially originally only accept
textual input which requires you to
convert all these documents into text
streams. So you basically see this here.
You start out with any raw document
format which can be a PDF which can be
an Excel which can be images. For some
of them it might be easier to convert
them to text. For others it might be
more difficult. That is basically
handled by your processing type pipeline
which takes all of these documents as
input and output text chunks which are
ideally equally sized which you can then
run through your embedding model to
generate the embedding.
So the question is now why is rag still
challenging? If you build rag system,
what you're definitely confronted with
the document format PDF is because it's
still the dominant document format in
enterprise um settings. The challenge is
that PDFs are display oriented, meaning
they are designed to look good if you
print them out or read them on the
screen. They're not designed to make the
data easy to extract. So converting a
PDF into text to then pass it to your
embedding model is a lossy
transformation. and visual information
gets lost or requires separate
processing.
There are obviously some cases where
it's easier to extract the textual
information. For example, for text heavy
reports which mostly contain linear text
from left to right, from top to bottom
with maybe some headers or footers. It
already starts to get more challenging
if you now have multicolumn layout. For
example, in scientific papers where you
start need need to think about reading
order.
It gets even more difficult if you now
have financial tables where you need to
align rows and columns. You need to
handle merge rows. Um and OCR solution
can easily misalign these. It also gets
more difficult if you think about slide
decks for example PowerPoint
presentations which are converted to PDF
because most of the information is
actually encoded visually and there's
might only be sparse text. Um, and it's
also getting more difficult for scanned
documents, which requires you to use an
OCR solution in the first place because
the text is not machine readable. And it
gets really difficult if you now want to
handle charts or infographics because
the meaning is purely visual and only
extracting the data labels of your
charts might not get you anywhere.
So how has this been originally handled?
So the classical approach is you start
with your PDF and you apply a layout
detection module which basically
segments the PDF or a page of the PDF
into text, figures, tables and so forth.
Then you run your OCR solution or text
extraction module to basically extract
the text from all of these segments.
And afterwards you recover the structure
of the document. So you basically want
to recover the reading order, you want
to process tables, and you want to merge
all of the texts. And this then gives
you a structured textual format of your
complete PDF document, which you can
then chunk into equally sized chunks,
embed, and store in your vector
database.
This works well for text heavy reports
as I already mentioned where for example
contracts, technical documentation, and
so on. Another advantage is that there's
a major ecos major e ecosystem with open
source options for PDF processing such
as pyu pdf or even complete OCR
solutions such as marker or dockling
also you have fine control fine grain
control over chunks overlap and other
hyperparameters.
However, it becomes more challenging if
you think about tables where OCR
solution might misalign rows or columns
as I already mentioned which would
produce wrong data assumptions. It also
becomes more challenging if you want to
reconstruct the reading order. So for
example, multicolumn uh multicolumn
documents might create garbled chunks if
the OCR solution misses that there are
two columns and just reads from left to
right which we've seen actually in
production quite many times even with
paid OCR solutions. It's also difficult
to capture charts because they are
mostly not handled by the OR solution.
So you need a separate processing layer
which handles your figures and charts
and you also lose the complete layout
information.
So the question I want to ask in this
presentation is what if we stopped
deconstructing documents into text and
instead embed them the way humans read
them as images.
So this was simplify the pipeline
actually a lot and this is possible due
to the rise of multimodel embedding
models. So you basically only take your
PDF you split it into different pages
from each page or even multiple page
pages you create an image and then you
embed only the image of the page
capturing all of the information that is
present.
So to start off I want to give you a
short overview of the landscapes of
models that are available. Just one
short thing to mention is I'm focusing
in this talk about B encoder models
which output single vectors. There's
also another family of models called
late interaction models which are mostly
included in academic benchmarks.
However, they're not really used in
practice uh in production settings

more storage because you need to save

the first model I want to mention here

images and both of them interled. It's a
proprietary RP and it's mainly
mentionable due to its large context
window and because it's fine-tuned for
finance, healthcare, and manufacturing.
A new addition to this list is Gemini
embedding 2, which is special because it

a proprietary RP. It's still in public
um preview and not generally available

Then there is voyage multimodel 3.5
which advertises itself with an
excellent uh matrioska representative
learning compression. For those of you

in brackets for for dimensions. It's
basically a learning scheme where the
vector vectors are trained in a way that
most of the information is encoded in
earlier dimensions which allows you to
cut off the vector at any point and only
for example retain the first 250 cy

you are guaranteed to use as little
quality as possible. So for example,
Voyage multimodel 3.5, they guarantee
that you only lose 1% of quality if you
only retain one quarter of the
dimensions, which can be quite nice in
production setting to save some costs.
[snorts]

images, the price is still much lower
compared to a complete OCR pipeline.
So the takeaway so far is embedding like
multimodel embedding models make the
pipeline much simpler and they can
reduce costs tremendously. So the final
question is are they any good? Can they
match the retrieval quality of an OCR
solution? And this is what I want to
look into next. And for this, I designed
a benchmark. Just a note, internally in

customer data first. But for the sake of
this presentation, because then I
couldn't have shared any real

evaluation with a public data set. So

PDFs

All right. So basically what can we take
away now? What are the trade-offs to
consider? So first of all what you gain
uh what you pay sorry what you pay is
page level granularity. So you retrieve
complete pages and not chunks and you I
mean you can control the chunk size by
for example embedding multiple PDF pages
into one image or something but mostly
you just need to take the pages as they
are. And the second and I think this is
maybe the crucial point is that you you
that you need to use a multimodel LLM
during generation time because all you
have during generation in the vector
database is a link to your image. So you
don't have the OCR solution with it
which extracted the text but you only
have the image. So during generation you
need to pass all these page images to
the um to the LLM as well. And this
basically requires the LLM to do the OCR
on the fly, which also likely requires
you to use a rather strong LLM. So you
might not be able to do this with very
small LLMs because again they need to
perform the OCR on the fly.
However, on the other side, what you
gain is a much simpler pipeline. You
don't need to worry about OCR, no layout
detection, no chunking. So it's very
fast to set up. You preserve all the
visual information by default. So all t
all tables, all charts and the complete
layout is preserved um the way humans
see them and usually the the documents
are at least currently still designed
for humans. Um this is all at much lower
costs and you usually have much higher
throughput. So usually your processing

separate processing modules for your
images where you need LLMs again and
then if you usually uploads 1,000
documents you need to worry about rate
limits and everything. So that is much
much better here assuming your embedding
model has a quite high throughput which
is usually the case. And this whole
thing is also formic agnostic. So it
doesn't only work for PDFs. You can also
use it for photos directly. You can use
it for word if you convert it to PDF.
You can use it for slides or whiteboard
photos. You simply render them as an
image and embed them.
All right. So I want to finish this talk
up with some practical guidelines. So,
first of all, I've always said um that

and can still look up the image for like

also enables you to use hybrid search if

The second point I want to make is how

And the thing I already mentioned is um

allow you to truncate the dimensions

And the final point is as I've did in
this benchmarks, it's always a good idea

just the generation quality because a

a good idea and usually costs you
nothing because you just need to
generate the retrieval data set once and
running the pipelines only occurs a few
embedding costs which are usually not
very high.
